Swarms

What animals compute together — and what we borrowed.

Nature → algorithms, and AI → nature.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A01 / 40

Opening puzzle

No ant is in charge. So who decides?

What one ant knows

  • A few centimetres of world
  • Simple local rules
  • No map
  • No idea what “the colony” is doing

What the colony does

  • Finds routes
  • Reallocates workers
  • Builds structures
  • Recovers from damage
Predict first · 90 sec

Propose one mechanism that turns local ignorance into global coordination. No leader allowed.

Almost every good answer is some form of signalling through the environment — a mark one ant leaves that changes what the next ant does. That is the next slide, and it has a name.

Opening puzzle

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A02 / 40

Core concept

Stigmergy: the environment becomes shared memory

Act

Do something local.

Mark

Leave a trace.

Sense

Another agent encounters it.

Amplify

Repeat and strengthen.

No negotiation. No central map. The world itself stores the coordination signal.

Coined by Pierre-Paul Grassé in 1959. Pheromone trails are the classic case; the same idea returns later in robot construction.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A03 / 40

Classic experiment

The double bridge: time creates an optimizer

1 · Explore
Both routes used

Ants initially spread across the long and short branches at random.

2 · Reinforce
Short trips lay trail more often

The round trip finishes sooner, so pheromone accumulates faster on the short branch.

3 · Recruit
Later ants prefer the stronger trail

Positive feedback: the trail that is used becomes the trail that is chosen.

4 · Converge
The colony settles

Almost all traffic takes the shorter path, though no ant ever compared the two.

The long route keeps a weaker trail throughout. Nothing was measured; time did the measuring.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A04 / 40

Nature → algorithm

Ant Colony Optimization: keep the loop, strip the biology

In the colony

  • An ant walks a route
  • Pheromone is deposited
  • Shorter routes reinforce faster
  • Pheromone evaporates
  • Future ants are biased by trail strength

In the algorithm

  • An agent builds a candidate solution
  • Good edges gain weight
  • Better solutions reinforce more
  • Weights decay
  • Future search is biased by learned weight

The transfer is structural, not anatomical.

Marco Dorigo, Ant System — 1992 doctoral thesis.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A05 / 40

Adaptability beats guarantees

Where ACO earns its keep

Vehicle routing

Many stops, time windows, changing constraints. The search must adapt as the day changes.

Network routing

Links fail and traffic shifts. A good path now may be bad minutes later.

Scheduling

The objective can be messy and discontinuous. Search quality matters more than closed-form elegance.

The honest limit

ACO is a metaheuristic. It rarely proves optimality and can lose to a specialized solver. Its strength is flexibility.

Ask of every bio-inspired algorithm: better than what, on which problem?

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A06 / 40
01

The swarm toolkit

Four coordination mechanisms, borrowed four different ways.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A07 / 40

Mechanism 2 · Flocking

Boids: three local rules can produce a flock

1
Separation

Avoid crowding immediate neighbours.

2
Alignment

Steer toward the average heading nearby.

3
Cohesion

Steer toward the local centre of mass.

No rule mentions “the flock.” The flock is the emergent outcome.

Craig Reynolds, “Flocks, Herds and Schools” — 1987.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A08 / 40

Think–pair–share

Emergence is what local rules add up to

What is in the rules

  • Distance to nearby neighbours
  • A heading to match
  • A direction to steer
  • No concept of flock shape

What appears anyway

  • Stable moving groups
  • Waves of turning
  • Split-and-rejoin around obstacles
  • Rapid collective response
Think · pair · share · 3 min

Name something in your life that looks centrally planned but is not. What is the local rule?

A traffic jam is the strongest answer: the jam travels backwards while every car moves forwards. The local rule is “brake when the car ahead brakes,” and nobody planned the wave. Queues, trends and applause all work the same way.
AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A09 / 40

Mechanism 3 · Social search

Particle Swarm Optimization

Scatter

Start widely across the space.

Evaluate

Score the current position.

Pull

Move toward personal best and group best.

Converge

Cluster on a peak.

Fast convergence is useful. Fast convergence to the wrong peak is not.

Kennedy and Eberhart, 1995 — inspired by bird flocking and human social behaviour.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A10 / 40

Mechanism 4 · Quorum

Honeybees hold something close to a debate

1
Scouts disperse

Independent bees inspect candidate nest sites.

2
Advertise in proportion

Waggle dances scale with perceived site quality.

3
Re-inspect

Recruits visit and judge for themselves.

4
Quorum triggers commitment

The colony commits when enough scouts gather at one site.

Independent verification protects the group from an early bandwagon.

Quorum sensing

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A11 / 40

Mechanism 5 · Grow then prune

A slime mould finds network structure without a brain

1 cell

Physarum has no nervous system

≈ Tokyo

network trade-offs resembled rail design

Explore broadly, strengthen useful tubes, prune the unused ones.

Careful with the headline: it did not “understand Tokyo.” It optimized a trade-off engineers also care about. Tero et al., Science, 2010.

Physarum

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A12 / 40

Compare the toolkit

Match the mechanism to the problem

Ants
Path

Feedback plus decay.

Birds
Move together

Local rules only.

Bees
Choose one option

Advertise, then verify.

Slime
Build network

Grow, then prune.

Group choice · 3 min

Flooded city: roads close unpredictably, and you must reroute emergency vehicles in real time. Which mechanism would you start from, and what would you borrow?

Ants for the routing — feedback plus decay handles roads that close and reopen. Slime mould if the question is which routes to keep open at all. The reasoning matters more than the choice; a defensible answer names what it borrows, not just which animal.

02

Robot swarms

From beautiful simulations to cheap, error-prone machines.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A14 / 40

Robot swarms

1,024 Kilobots: scale without micromanagement

1,024

robots in one swarm

Local

infrared neighbour sensing only

Each robot is simple, myopic and imperfect. Together they assemble a target shape and correct local mistakes.

The engineering achievement is tolerance of hardware failure, not raw robot count. Rubenstein, Cornejo and Nagpal, Science, 2014.

Kilobots

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A15 / 40

Stigmergy in bricks

TERMES: build without a foreman

The termite idea
The structure tells the next worker what to do

No central supervisor, and robots read only local structure.

The consequence
Robots can join or leave mid-build

Adding or removing a robot does not restart the plan — the site is the shared plan.

Stigmergy returns: pheromone becomes bricks. Werfel, Petersen and Nagpal, Science, 2014.

TERMES

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A16 / 40

Architecture test

What counts as a real swarm?

Looks like a swarm

  • Hundreds of drones
  • Coordinated formations
  • Precise synchronization
  • Often one central plan plus GPS

Acts like a swarm

  • Local sensing or peer communication
  • No single point of failure
  • Collective pattern emerges
  • Degrades gracefully when units fail
Vote · 2 min

A drone light show: swarm or not?

Not. It is visually swarm-like and architecturally almost the opposite — one central plan, GPS, and a single point of failure. The test for any “swarm” product: what happens when the central link goes down?
AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A17 / 40

Costs and limits

Decentralization is a trade, not an upgrade

1
No guarantees

Emergent systems can be hard to prove correct.

2
Hard to debug

The failure may live in the interactions, not in any one agent.

3
Tuning is fiddly

Neighbour radii, decay and weights can change behaviour sharply.

4
What you gain

Graceful scaling, and no single failure point.

Swarm: capability degrades gradually. Centralized: one failure can cascade.

03

AI as an instrument

The direction reverses: now we use AI to listen, watch and count.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A19 / 40

Bioacoustics

BirdNET: recorders never sleep, but humans cannot listen to everything

Deploy

Autonomous recorders left in the field.

Accumulate

More audio than people can hear.

Classify

Species identified from sound.

Monitor

Presence tracked over time.

Hours become months of sound. The app matters because a research model became public infrastructure.

Citizen science expands where and what gets observed. Kahl et al.; Wood et al., PLOS Biology, 2022.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A20 / 40

Project CETI

Sperm whales: structure found, meaning not yet decoded

≈9k

codas in the 2024 study

4

features: rhythm, tempo, rubato, ornamentation

A much richer combinatorial structure than previously recognized.

The sentence headlines often drop: the communicative function of many codas remains unknown. Sharma et al., Nature Communications, 2024.

Project CETI

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A21 / 40

Rank the evidence

What would convince you we decoded an animal signal?

A
Patterns like language

Recurring units, combinations, something like grammar.

B
Correlates with behaviour

A call reliably appears before a context or action.

C
Works in playback

Playing the signal produces the predicted response.

Rank and defend · 4 min

Order A, B and C from weakest to strongest. Then say what could still be wrong about your strongest one.

Usually A → B → C. But playback is confoundable too: an animal may respond to a startling noise rather than to meaning, and a played-back call carries no speaker, no context and no history. Naming that objection is the exercise.
AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A22 / 40

Computer vision in ecology

Camera traps turn rare encounters into a searchable dataset

Trigger

Motion captures a frame.

Detect

Find animals; discard empty frames.

Classify

Species and count.

Review

A human checks the uncertain cases.

The AI does not replace the ecologist. It triages millions of frames so human attention goes where it matters.

The same division of labour as radiology: the machine narrows the queue, the expert owns the conclusion.

Camera trap

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A23 / 40

Identity at scale

Recognize the individual, not just the species

Natural fingerprints
Flukes, stripes, patches and fins

Whale flukes, zebra stripes, giraffe patches, tiger stripes and shark fins can be individually distinctive.

Why it matters
Questions that need the same animal twice

Population size, survival, movement and social structure.

A tourist photograph can become a longitudinal population data point.

Individual ID

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A24 / 40

Conservation in practice

From detecting animals to protecting them

1
Patrol planning

Predict where poaching risk is high and allocate scarce ranger effort.

2
Acoustic alerts

Listen for chainsaws, gunshots or vessels and flag them quickly.

3
Collision avoidance

Detect whales near shipping lanes so vessels can slow or reroute.

4
The bottleneck

Detection is cheap. Response is not. An alert without people, boats or budget changes nothing.

AI can move the bottleneck. It cannot guarantee the bottleneck disappears.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A25 / 40

The borrowing runs both ways

Now AI is used to infer the rules animals actually follow

Track

Every individual, continuously.

Model

Who responds to whom.

Infer

Candidate local rules.

Test

Compare against real behaviour.

Boids was a useful guess. Modern tracking lets us ask whether real flocks use similar local rules.

Abstract → build → measure → revise: the same scientific loop as the neuroscience lecture.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A26 / 40
04

Limits and ethics

Cheap sensing plus good models means continuous observation of wild things.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A27 / 40

Limit 1 · Data

Ecological data breaks the assumptions models like

1
Long tail

Common species dominate the data; rare species have the fewest examples.

2
Geographic bias

Observations cluster where researchers, roads and tourists are.

3
Field noise

Wind, rain, occlusion, overlapping calls, darkness and distance.

4
Shifting baseline

Climate and land use change the distribution the model was trained on.

The species that matter most can be exactly the ones a model knows least about.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A28 / 40

False positives vs missed rarity

When is an alert worth acting on?

Miss a real animal

  • A rare species goes undetected
  • A poaching event is missed
  • Collision risk persists
  • The failure may remain invisible

Raise a false alarm

  • Ranger time is wasted
  • Ships may reroute unnecessarily
  • Trust in the system erodes
  • The failure is immediate and visible
Set threshold · 3 min

Your model outputs a probability. Where do you set the alert threshold, and who should decide?

The threshold encodes a value judgement about whose costs count — and it is usually set by whoever built the model, by default. Notice the asymmetry: one failure mode is invisible and compounds, the other is visible and immediate, which biases institutions toward the wrong one.
AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A29 / 40

Scientific discipline

Structure found is not meaning decoded

Observation

  • “This coda contains recurring combinatorial structure.”
  • Measurable
  • Reproducible
  • Testable

Interpretation

  • “The whale said: let’s go home.”
  • Possible someday
  • Not established by structure alone
  • A story the structure permits, not one it supports

AI can make patterns visible. Humans still have to separate evidence from story.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A30 / 40

Ethics

What do we owe the animals we can now watch continuously?

Disturbance

Sensors and tags can change behaviour. Better measurement is not automatically harmless.

Data ownership

Who controls location data for endangered or culturally important species?

Dual use

A map that helps conservation can also help poachers or extractive industries.

The question is no longer “can we observe?” It is who gets to observe, for what purpose, and with what safeguards.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A31 / 40
05

Transferable ideas

Four principles that survive when the biology is removed.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A32 / 40

Principle 1

Reinforcement needs forgetting

Discover

Find something useful.

Reinforce

Make it easier to repeat.

Decay

Let stale evidence fade.

Adapt

Shift when the world changes.

Without decay, early accidents become permanent beliefs.

Pheromone evaporation is not a nuisance — it is the mechanism that lets the colony forget. Transfers to recommendation systems, routing, memory and online learning.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A33 / 40

Principle 2

Robustness can come from ignorance

Less information

Each unit senses only what it needs locally.

Fewer failure modes

No global map or controller that everyone depends on.

Graceful scale

The same rule can run with ten agents or a thousand.

Centralized systems know more. Decentralized systems may survive more.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A34 / 40

Principle 3

Group wisdom requires independent judgment

Advertise

Share a candidate.

Verify

Others inspect independently.

Commit

Quorum, not mere copying.

Result

Less bandwagon risk.

A crowd of copiers is not wise, however large.

This is why model ensembles help only when their members make different mistakes.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A35 / 40

Principle 4

Borrow the mechanism, not the appearance

What transferred

  • Feedback plus decay, from ant trails
  • Local rules, from flocks
  • Advertise plus verify, from bee swarms
  • Grow plus prune, from slime mould

What did not

  • Chemistry, legs, wings, cell biology
  • The organism’s appearance
  • Its evolutionary history
  • Any claim that the algorithm is how biology really works

The artificial neuron taught the same lesson: useful abstractions are principles, not anatomical copies.

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A36 / 40

Synthesis challenge

Design a swarm: your turn

Brief — map a coral reef with 200 cheap underwater drones. Individually unreliable, short battery life, patchy communication, no GPS.

Decide 1
Local rule

What does one drone sense, and what does it do next?

Decide 2
What decays?

What forgetting mechanism prevents over-surveying the first interesting region?

Decide 3
Failure test

What happens when half the drones fail?

Groups of four · 7 min

Sketch your rule and your decay, then answer the failure test honestly.

If the answer to the failure test is “it stops”, the design is centralized wearing a swarm costume. A real swarm answers: coverage slows, resolution drops, the map still completes.
AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A37 / 40

Report out

Your swarm in the world

1 & 2
The rule and the decay

State each in one sentence a classmate could implement.

3
Fifty per cent failure

What the swarm still does when half the units are gone.

4
The honest one

One failure mode you still cannot prevent.

The fourth is the one worth listening to. Every design has one.

Report out

AI × Nature · Swarms · Lecture 6A39 / 40

Takeaway

Intelligence does not require a single intelligent thing

01 · MECHANISMFeedback with decay, local rules, independent verification, grow then prune
02 · INSTRUMENTAI now listens, watches and counts on a scale field biology never had
03 · DISCIPLINEPattern is not meaning. A confident label is not an observation
Exit ticket · 2 min

Name one system you use that reinforces without forgetting. What should its evaporation rate be?

Recommendation feeds, reputation scores, citation counts and search rankings all reinforce without decay — which is why an early accident can become a permanent belief. The interesting half of the answer is who would have to set that rate, and whether they want to.

Sources: Dorigo (1992); Reynolds (1987); Kennedy & Eberhart (1995); Tero et al. (2010); Wyss/Science (2014); BirdNET; Project CETI.
